variants.name: asyncio task cancellation
variants.implementation_notes: In asyncio the task is the token: Task.cancel() schedules a CancelledError at the task's next await, the coroutine must let it propagate (or clean up and re-raise), and asyncio.shield protects a nested awaitable that must finish. Deadlines derive cancellation - asyncio.timeout()/asyncio.wait_for cancel the current task and translate the result into TimeoutError - and TaskGroup/gather propagate a cancel between siblings according to their documented rules. Cancellation is edge-based: it is delivered once at a suspension point and the task may even suppress it, which is why the re-raise rule matters. For synchronous code the stdlib has no equivalent and a threading.Event flag is the fallback.
variants.code_sketch:
task = asyncio.create_task(worker(item))
...
task.cancel()                            # request

try:
    await task                           # raises CancelledError when it stops
except asyncio.CancelledError:
    log.info("cancelled")
    raise                                # never swallow cancellation
pitfalls: Swallowing CancelledError (or catching Exception around awaits and continuing) leaves the task running in a cancelled state; since Python 3.8 CancelledError derives from BaseException, so bare except Exception no longer catches it, but an explicit catch-and-continue still breaks the contract.
Cancellation is delivered only at await points: a CPU-bound block between awaits ignores it, so offload heavy work or check asyncio.current_task().cancelling() explicitly.

asyncio.shield protects the inner awaitable but the awaiting coroutine still receives CancelledError, and a wait_for timeout cancels the shielded caller while the shielded work continues - a common source of orphaned tasks.

Task.cancel() is a request: the task may finish normally or ignore it, so code that must be sure of the outcome has to await the task (and a task reference must be kept, since the loop only holds weak references).

variants.name: anyio/trio cancel scopes (level cancellation)
variants.implementation_notes: The structured-concurrency frameworks model cancellation as a scope rather than a single delivery: a CancelScope is a context manager that can be cancelled as a unit, every task inside an effectively cancelled scope is cancelled at each yield point (level cancellation), and a task group owns its own scope so cancelling the group cancels all its tasks. move_on_after/fail_after turn timeouts into cancel scopes with a deadline, shield=True carves out a region that must finish (shutdown/cleanup), and CancelScope.cancel(reason) records why. This is strictly stronger than asyncio's edge cancellation because a suppressed exception does not escape the scope, and the re-raise rule still applies to cancellation exceptions.
variants.code_sketch:
async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
    with anyio.move_on_after(2) as scope:        # deadline becomes cancellation
        tg.start_soon(step, item)
    if scope.cancelled_caught:
        log.info("budget exhausted")

tg.cancel_scope.cancel()                         # cancel the whole group
pitfalls: Cancel scopes must be entered and exited in LIFO order per task: yielding from inside a scope (async generators, manual __enter__) corrupts the stack and produces hard-to-diagnose behaviour.

Catching the framework's cancellation exception requires get_cancelled_exc_class(), since the class differs per backend; catching Exception instead is wrong in both directions and any caught cancellation must be re-raised.
Cleanup that awaits inside an already cancelled scope is cancelled immediately: wrap it in a shielded scope (or CancelScope(shield=True)) or the resource never closes.
Cancelling a scope from a task that does not own it, or cancelling a fail_after scope directly, produces misleading TimeoutErrors - cancel the task group's scope instead.

variants.name: threading.Event flag for synchronous threads
variants.idiom_name: shared threading.Event checked in the loop, with Event.wait(timeout) as the interruptible wait
variants.implementation_notes: Synchronous Python has no way to stop a thread: the threading documentation is explicit that threads cannot be destroyed, stopped, suspended or interrupted, so the token is a hand-written threading.Event (or a bounded queue) that the worker checks each iteration and a timed wait that lets a blocked worker wake and re-check. Blocking calls must be bounded - Event.wait(timeout), Queue.get(timeout=...), socket timeouts, executor futures with timeouts - because an unbounded call never reaches a safe point. The pattern still works, but the payload of checking is on the library author rather than the runtime.
pitfalls: An unbounded blocking call (queue.get() without timeout, socket without timeout, lock.acquire() without timeout) makes the flag invisible and the worker unresponsive - bound every wait.
Set the event before joining and keep the flag per operation tree: a module-level event cancels every worker that shares it, including unrelated pools.
The GIL does not make compound checks atomic: reading a plain boolean set by another thread is a race in principle and Event/Lock is the supported primitive.
Threads that are already blocked in uninterruptible native code cannot be rescued by any flag; such work must be isolated in a process or moved to a library with timeouts and cancellation.
